article.headline: The Near-Overhead Sun That Turns Bare Branches Into a Mandala
article.lede: A photograph circulating on social media shows a nearly leafless urban tree whose bare branches cast a perfectly radial, circular shadow across the surrounding pavement — every twig pointing outward from the trunk simultaneously, like a diagram of an underground root system laid flat on concrete. The image is disorienting because it contradicts the intuition that shadows extend in a single direction. What produces it is elementary solar geometry, a near-vertical sun, and the hidden symmetry of how trees grow.
article.body:
The key is the sun's angle. Shadow length is proportional to an object's height divided by the tangent of the sun's elevation above the horizon. As that angle climbs toward 90°, the tangent approaches infinity and shadows shrink toward zero — simple trigonometry. A tree's branches extend outward from the trunk in every horizontal direction; when the sun sits nearly overhead, each branch throws its shadow almost straight down, projecting radially outward from the trunk's base. The result is symmetry in all directions: a crown that at any other hour would cast a single elongated blob throws, at near-vertical noon, a burst pattern indistinguishable from a botanical illustration.

The location reinforces the effect. The image appears to have been taken at a low tropical latitude — consistent with central Mexico, which lies at roughly 19°N, well inside the band between the tropics where the sun passes directly overhead twice each year. That annual moment is called *zero-shadow day*, or in Hawaii *Lāhainā Noon*, when a vertical post casts no outward shadow at all. The photograph was posted in mid-May, just weeks after the late-April overhead-sun date for that latitude; the midday sun would have stood at perhaps 85° of elevation. Even outside the tropics the effect is visible around summer-solstice noon in mid-latitude cities — just less extreme.

What lifts the image beyond a geometry demonstration is its uncanny resemblance to an underground root system. That resemblance is not coincidental. Both branches and roots follow the same **fractal branching** logic — a self-similar pattern in which each large branch subdivides into smaller ones at a constant proportional ratio, repeatedly, down to the finest twigs. Around 1490, Leonardo da Vinci observed that at every branch point, the combined cross-sectional area of the daughter branches equals the area of the parent branch — a rule that preserves total conducting capacity for water throughout the tree. Modern biomechanics extends this: branching angles and thickness ratios also distribute mechanical stress uniformly, for the same structural reasons that apply underground. Because the same optimization pressures act on roots, root systems and canopies converge on nearly identical geometries — which is precisely why the shadow, projected flat onto pavement, looks as if it belongs below ground rather than above it.

The soft blur at each twig's shadow edge is not diffraction but *penumbra*: the sun is not a geometric point but a disk spanning roughly 0.5° of arc. Light from one side of that disk is blocked by a branch while light from the opposite side still reaches the ground, producing a gradient fringe around the shadow's hard core. The effect grows with distance from the branch, so twigs far from the trunk cast fuzzier shadows than those close to it — adding a subtle depth cue that reinforces the three-dimensional impression of the whole.

concepts.definition: Twice a year at any location between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, the sun passes directly overhead at local solar noon, causing vertical objects to cast no outward shadow. In Hawaii the moment is called Lāhainā Noon; in India it is widely used as a school-science event. Outside the tropics the sun never reaches true zenith, but high summer-noon elevations create a near-equivalent effect on shadow patterns.

The Hawaiian name for zero-shadow day, named for the former whaling port of Lāhainā on Maui. Twice yearly, at local solar noon, the sun stands directly overhead and vertical objects cast no shadow. The Bishop Museum in Honolulu has long used the event as a public-outreach moment for solar geometry.

A self-similar structural pattern in which a system subdivides repeatedly at the same proportional ratio across many scales, producing similar-looking geometry whether examined up close or from a distance. Trees, river deltas, lung airways, and root systems all exhibit fractal branching because it solves the same structural and fluid-transport optimization problem at every scale.

An observation recorded by Leonardo da Vinci around 1490: at every branch point in a tree, the combined cross-sectional area of the daughter branches equals the cross-sectional area of the parent. The rule predicts that total conducting capacity for water is conserved throughout the tree, and it explains why above-ground and below-ground branching converge on nearly identical geometries.

The zone of partial shadow surrounding the fully dark core (umbra) of a shadow, produced because the light source has a finite angular width rather than being a perfect geometric point. In sunlight, the penumbra around a twig's shadow widens with distance from the branch, since more of the sun's disk can be partially obscured at greater distances.

The angle between the sun and the horizon, measured in degrees. At sunrise and sunset it is 0°; at local noon it peaks, reaching 90° only at tropical latitudes during zero-shadow day. Shadow length is inversely related to the tangent of this angle: a higher sun produces shorter shadows, approaching zero length as the angle approaches 90°.

sources.title: Shadows and the Sun — The Nature Institute
sources.note: Primary explanation of how tree-branch shadows form and why the sun's angular disk (not diffraction) governs shadow softness and radial pattern

sources.title: How Does Diffraction Make a Tree's Shadow Blurry? — West Texas A&M University
sources.note: Rules out diffraction; confirms extended solar disk as the cause of penumbra around branch shadows

sources.title: Zero shadow day — Wikipedia
sources.note: Background on the twice-yearly zero-shadow event at tropical latitudes, including the Lāhainā Noon variant and its geometry

sources.title: Zero-Shadow Day Makes This Picture Look Strange — AccuWeather
sources.note: Covers near-zenith sun visual effects, including the Isamu Noguchi Sky Gate sculpture casting a perfect circle during zero-shadow day

sources.title: Tree Fractals — Gabriel Hemery
sources.note: Accessible explanation of da Vinci's branching rule, fractal self-similarity in tree architecture, and the mirror between roots and canopy

sources.title: Leonardo's Rule, Self-Similarity, and Wind-Induced Stresses in Trees — PLoS ONE / PMC
sources.note: Peer-reviewed analysis of da Vinci's rule versus biomechanical stress models; explains why branch and root geometry converge

sources.title: Branch Scaling and Art — PNAS Nexus
sources.note: Quantitative study of fractal branch-radius scaling across species; shows self-similar geometry holds from trunk to finest twigs

sources.title: Types of Tree-Form Shadow Pattern — ResearchGate
sources.note: Scientific documentation of how crown architecture and sun angle interact to produce distinct on-ground shadow patterns

poster_rainmaker1973.blurb: Engineer and curator of captivating content since 2014, Massimo (@Rainmaker1973) shares threads and posts on science, technology, art, weather, space, and unusual phenomena. With a mission to awaken a sense of wonder, he has amassed a large following on X. His threads, such as '15 facts about Greenland' and 'Vintage elevators,' showcase his knack for distilling fascinating topics into engaging, bite-sized insights.
